preamble: Lowering of the close front rounded vowel [y] to the close-mid [ø]. In Swedish, the Old East Norse short vowels were lengthened in short stressed syllables, and the high vowels were lowered as they lengthened: short y gave long /øː/, as in Old Norse kyn 'kin, kind' > kön /ɕøːn/ and fyl 'foal' > föl, while short y that stayed short is now /ʏ/ or /œ/. Old Swedish already writes køn beside kyn. Wikipedia's Open syllable lengthening reports the same lowering of short /y/ to /ø/ in Old Danish, before its lengthening (Old Norse fyl > Danish føl [ˈføl]), and gives Old Dutch y > Middle Dutch lengthened ø̄; Wikipedia's Middle Dutch writes that step as lengthened [ʏː] > [øː]. In Tatar, the Old Turkic high vowels became a reduced mid series (Johanson 1998, as summarized by Wikipedia): *ü became ө, a reduced [ø̆~ɵ̆], as in *kül 'ash' > köl, while the mid vowel *ö was raised to ү (ø → y).

examples.from: Old Norse kyn 'kin, kind' (Old Swedish kyn, køn)
Old Norse yfir 'over' (Old Swedish ivir, yvir, ø̄wer)

examples.note: Wikipedia's Tatar vowel chart gives ө as a reduced mid [ø̆~ɵ̆]. Bashkir spells the same words көл and көн, but Wiktionary transcribes them [kʏ̞l] and /kʏ̞n/, and Bashkir is not listed here. Wikipedia's Bashkir phonology argues that in both Bashkir and Tatar the old near-close vowels remained in place, adding that the Tatar reduced series is closer to the Chuvash one; this entry follows the Tatar article's summary of Johanson (1998), as u → o does for Tatar *u > о.
